subject: music
title: Clefs, Time and Key Signatures
welcome_lead: Treble, bass, alto and tenor — and how to read them.
meta_desc: A-Level Music: clefs, time signatures, and key signatures.
final_note: The clef points to a fixed pitch.

concepts.def: G clef — line through curl is G4.
F clef — dots above/below line for F3.
C clef centred on middle C (used by viola).
C clef on 4th line (used by upper bassoon, trombone, cello).
Upper number = beats per bar; lower = unit of beat.
Sharps or flats appearing at the start of each line.

walkthroughs.body_html: Alto clef (viola) centres middle C on the middle line. Tenor clef (bassoon, trombone, cello upper register) puts middle C on the 4th line. Both are 'movable C clefs'.
Simple time (2/4, 3/4, 4/4): beat divides into 2. Compound (6/8, 9/8, 12/8): beat divides into 3. Top number divides by 3 to give compound beats per bar.
Sharps appear in order F-C-G-D-A-E-B; flats in reverse B-E-A-D-G-C-F. Major key with one sharp = G major; with one flat = F major.

Simple
Compound
Irregular
Asymmetric

mcqs.q: What does the time signature 6/8 indicate?
options: Percussion.
Two beats per bar, each beat divided into three (compound duple).
A piece six bars long.
Six beats per bar, all equal in stress.

mcqs.q: How do you identify a major key from its key signature?
options: Percussion.
It is always C major.
The last sharp is the leading note (semitone below tonic); the second-to-last flat is the tonic.
The number of sharps or flats equals the tonic note number.

mcqs.q: Which orchestral family does the saxophone belong to?
options: It is always C major.
Percussion.
Brass (because it is made of brass).
Woodwind.
